newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE - Pakistan railways on losing track.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pakistan railways on losing track.

text.p: The Pakistani government is preparing to apply brakes to the money being lost by Pakistan Railways by selling it off in small chunks to private operators.

"Privatisation (of railways) can lessen the financial burden on the limited resources of the government of Pakistan," Mohammad Afzal Khan, general manager of Pakistan Railways, told a privatisation seminar in Islamabad recently.
"By providing efficient means of transport, a private railway industry shall provide an impetus to the economic activities of the country," he added.
A government official, who asked not to be named, said a specially constituted task force had been asked to restructure the organisation by the end of this year.

"It has been asked to restructure the railways, cut down labour, break it into passenger, freight and other companies and lay out the regulatory framework to allow for private companies to run railways," the official added.
RECOMMENDATIONS TO BE IMPLEMENTED IN FULL
The recommendations of the task force, constituted in March by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, were discussed recently and it was decided to implement them in full, he added.
The target is to bring corporate culture into railways, which had been running as a public utility and incurring losses for several years.
"Pakistan Railways generated a surplus of 85 million rupees in the financial year 1971-72 (July-June)," Khan said.
"The position, however, changed in the succeeding years as the expenditure increased in disproportionate ratio compared to the increase in tariff," he added.

Khan said railways generated 9.5 billion rupees' revenue against an expenditure of 13.39 billion rupees in fiscal 1996/97 compared to 8.13 billion rupees' revenue and 15.5 billion rupees' expenditure in 1995/96.
The gap between the revenue and expenditure had forced the railways to borrow from the State (central) Bank of Pakistan at an interest rate of 15 percent at different times, he said.
"In June, 1997, the overdraft was 9.7 billion rupees and the burden of interest alone during 1996/97 was 1.0 billion rupees approximately," he added.
HIGH WAGE COSTS
The task force has also been entrusted to cut the huge work force of 104,000 employees, described as surplus by various government studies.

"The Railways is presently spending more than 85 percent of its total revenue budget on items like wages, pension, fuel, electricity and hardly 15 percent is left for the maintenance of its infrastructure, thereby seriously affecting the efficiency of operations," Khan said.
"The existing fleet of goods wagons is of slow speed and pre-World War-II design.

"Introduction of high-speed, high-capacity wagons which could move at 100 km (62 miles) per hour would have reduced journey time, increased sectional capacity and reduced requirements of locomotives, and this would have been cost effective."
The task force has been told to move passenger traffic into a separate company from freight traffic.

Khan said railways' share of passenger traffic had declined to 10.4 percent from 11.05 percent in 1992/93 against road and air travel and of freight to 12.62 percent in 1994/95 from 14.3 percent in 1992/93.
The length of railway track in Pakistan had shrunk to 7,788 km (4,876 miles) compared to 8,577 km (5,360 miles) in 1947 when Pakistan gained independence from Britain.
